So even in the case where we already had photographs from other sources, the IMG data served to corroborate that. It was a professionally run organisation, serving mainly the needs of the European Union, which was tasked with making assessments for reconstruction in Kosovo. The implementation on the local level was somewhat uneven, as I note in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, while we are with this mosque in Brestovac, Orahovac municipality, from what I see you used only the photograph of Sabri Bajgora from 1999. What does the reference "IMG Database" mean? Where are the photographs from that group?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take a look at my expert report, you will see that the -- for technical reasons, we could not extract the photographs from the IMG database and insert them into this report, and so we submitted a CD with the IMG database along with the report. So the fact that we are only showing one photograph doesn't include -- imply necessarily that we have only one. Also, in order to limit the size of the database, we tried to put in the minimum number of photographs. If you put in too many, the database slows down and becomes hard to operate. So, in many of these cases, the number of photographs you see in the database entry is only a subset of the number of photographs that were available to us when we're making our assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That CD is confined to the IMG database, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, does that have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's a separate item that we have not submitted to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, would you also agree with me that you did not perform a direct assessment of the mosque in Velika Krusa either?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that for this mosque, again -- no, strike that. For this mosque, you, again, have a report from the human rights group, without naming the person who provided the report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: 1776, an exhibit, P1776.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have our assessment that it's heavily damaged, and - if you can scroll down, please - you can see the description that the minaret's blown up. There's a large hole in the side wall, structural damage; interior of the mosque is vandalised and partially burned. That was the extent of our assessment. And, you know, any informant statements are merely supplementary, to be taken for whatever value the Court chooses to assign to them. You can also see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is, perhaps, a good example to clarify the role of Sabri Bajgora. To what extent was the conversation between you and him about the nature of the damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, we -- well, on our three visits to Kosovo, I visited the offices of the Islamic community each time. Each time I came away with a bag full of photographs. We had, in each case, a several-hour conversation, during which I took notes. As he handed me the photographs, he would identify what they were and, in some cases, say things about them, you know, when it was destroyed or when it had been built. He was speaking from his own notes. He didn't hand me any kind of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But when you conclude "minaret blown up, leaving a large hole in side wall of the mosque and structural damage" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my own conclusion from looking at this photo. You can see the stump of a minaret and you can see big cracks in the building radiating from where the minaret used to be, which, to me, having seen many dozens of such buildings, indicates that there was some kind of internal blast in the minaret causing this. You can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mr. Riedlmayer. But can I take it that that was your approach in every case, to make an independent assessment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- from the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If there's outside sources, I usually tried to indicate where that information came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'm now interested in P1777, which is a Prosecution exhibit. I see that you personally made the assessment of this building, with due respect to every building in every community. I see that this one was built in 1997, two years before the war. To what extent does it constitute a cultural and historic monument?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a house of worship and, as such, it served a cultural purpose. I don't think a building has to be centuries old to be a cultural monument. And, as I also noted, in the list of monuments granted legally protected status in Kosovo under the Yugoslav administration, there were any number of buildings that were of no great antiquity. I'm thinking, for example, the church built in Djakovica on the various eve of the war, which is almost the same age as this building. It was a memorial church for Serbian war dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, although this question may have sounded not sufficiently serious, initially this is precisely the reason why I put it. When you said that the list was coloured by politics and ideology, you gave an examples saying that some buildings, built between 1930 and 1990, were put on the list. This, if I'm not wrong, was also one of the reasons why you challenged the list.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I challenged the list nearly on the basis that the number and age of Islamic monuments in Kosovo would have suggested that more than 15 might have qualified; and, in fact, they did not. And given that things like state money for reconstruction and conservation work depended on this official status, I considered that to have been ideological potentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. Riedlmayer, that the mosque in Cirez, Srbica municipality, is another one which you did not inspect personally? That's 1778, Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you have no information from citizens or newspaper reports concerning this mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I can describe is its condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct, Mr. Riedlmayer - and this is Prosecution Exhibit 1785 concerning the mosque in Vlastica - that you did not visit this site either or inspect it personally?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in your report no report by citizens is listed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would now like to know, Mr. Riedlmayer, on what basis you wrote that the village was the scene of a crime committed by Serb forces in the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll down so I can see what I actually wrote. Okay. I was merely repeating the information that was in the indictment, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were using the indictment against Milosevic when compiling this. Do you remember I asked you that before, and you now seem to be confirming that you used the Milosevic indictment.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm saying. In fact, if we had been using the Milosevic indictment as a guideline to -- for sites to visit, we surely would have visited these particular sites. No. In the final stage of compiling the report, we thought it might be helpful for the OTP, for whom we were giving this report, to note the sites which pertained to their indictment. It was, you know, an attempt to be helpful, that's all. But we didn't use the indictment as our guideline.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So where it says that the village was the site of an atrocity by Serb forces, you were trying to help the OTP and support the indictment. Is that the only reason why you included this? Let me ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Page 49, line 10 of the transcript, you said that you were repeating the information in the indictment; that this could be useful for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was merely noting which sites might be of interest to them. It was probably foolish because they could have done that work themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's not consistent because you didn't do it in every case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the final indictment was actually issued after we submitted this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the indictment you had access to one which had only one accused on it, or did it have more than one accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we submitted this report in, I believe, September of 2001. The final amended indictment was issued in October of 2001. So we used whatever would have been available as of early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Riedlmayer, is it also correct that you did not inspect the mosque in Kacanik? That's P1786.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you bring it up on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is such a waste of time, Mr. Bakrac, because we know he didn't from the report itself. If there's another particular question to be put, then we could move on to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a question. I may have missed it, but I don't see a photograph here. It doesn't say who inspected the site. There's no photograph, no citizen's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's quite clear there was a photograph from this IMG database. So you know what the source of the information is. Now, you may have a point to make later that the Prosecution haven't bothered to provide us with the database. There's possible a good argument for you in closing arguments, but where are we going with the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's precisely my intention. I don't know how the inspection was conducted. We don't see the church or mosque. We can't check what kind of damage there was. We don't know what can be seen on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Mr. Hannis will, no doubt, point to other evidence about this mosque as well. So you've got to take account of everything that relates to it in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honour, I'm now only asking for Exhibit P1788 to be put on the screen. It's a photograph of this mosque. Or rather, I do apologise. My assistant is now telling me that it's actually P1799. Could we have that on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you said that this was the market mosque in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And this pre-war photograph was one you compared with the photograph you took on site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I assume that you made an effort to take the second photograph from the same vantage point that the first was taken from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in this case, I wish I had, but I just got lucky. Vucitrn was the very first site we visited in Kosovo, and I didn't have Mr. Virmica's photos until several days later when we visited Prizren, which is where he lives. So it just happened that I happened to have a photograph that shows approximately the same vantage point. At the time I was there, I was not in possession of the pre-war photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 2 of this exhibit. But before that, I withdraw that -- sorry, I have one more. Could we have the previous page again, please, to clear up one more detail with Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, there's a tall residential building to the left of the mosque, and you stated that this was an identifying element. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that both this building and the mosque, or rather, that the right-hand wall, the right-hand edge of the building, is parallel to the left-hand edge of the mosque and that there is a space in between? The two walls are practically parallel, and the mosque is on the -- to the right of the wall of this building.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, but the residential building is considerably in the back. It is much further from the viewer than the mosque is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, if I remember well, yesterday, when you were explaining the second photograph, you pointed to an entrance. Would you agree that the entrance to the mosque was facing the building that you say is an identifying element?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If this photograph were clearer, you would see that the mosque, which is actually an old building, has had a modern entrance structure added to it, facing the photographer here. It's got two steps side -- on either side there are steps leading up to it. The minaret is to the right of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now please show us page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, do you recognise in the background --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same building, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, if we established on the previous photograph that the right wall of this tall building is parallel to the left wall of the mosque, that the mosque would have to be completely outside the frame of this photograph? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. There's a lack of foundation for that question. We don't know which camera was used and what angle each of the photos were taken. All kinds of things don't support that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm satisfied that there's an adequate foundation and that the witness will be able to deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if you look at picture number 1, it was taken at some distance and down hill. This is much closer to the building. It is very hard to orient oneself in the field of rubble, but if you move back to the previous photograph, photograph 1 of this set - could you do that, please; yes - the elements that I was able to identify were parts of the ablution fountain, which is separate from the mosque, and the large utility pole, which was lying across the site with one side very charred, and pieces of rubble, which had carved and painted elements which, I assume, came from the mosque. But since everything had been graded by heavy machinery, identifying particular points within the site was very difficult. In addition to the mosque, you can see there were low buildings surrounding it on the rear. Those were parts of the Carshia, the traditional goldsmith's bazaar, which, according to our information - and we cite the name of the informant - had been burned down and pillaged the same time that the mosque was burned down. I was there at the site. I can vouch for the fact that, you know, there is no mosque there now, or at least wasn't in October of 1999. It may have been re-built since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, to help understand this point, can you explain what your case is on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday, the witness identifying the photograph had pointed to the spot where the mosque had been located. The Defence is convinced that the ruin shown by the witness cannot be the correct area, in the correct area, because, looking at this photograph, it's evident that the mosque is to the right, below the road, and that the ruins marked by the witness as the ruins of the mosque cannot, in fact, be the ruins of the mosque, in view of their location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the point isn't that there's something odd about the photograph; the point is that the mosque may well have been destroyed but its ruins are not what the witness examined. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I interject something? As I look more closely at the pre-war photo, you will see the fenced-in ablution fountain to the left of the mosque, which also has a set of low concrete steps. It may well be that I mistook the foundations of the ablution fountain in the post-war photo for the foundations of the mosque proper. But I can vouch for the fact that where the mosque used to be there was only rubble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, are you aware how many historical monuments of Serb culture were destroyed after the departure of the Serb forces from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I list them in my database, where the number that I cite and the number cited by the Serbian Orthodox church, in its publication "Rasveta Kosovo," are roughly the same, 80. Of these 80, roughly half were lightly damaged or vandalised, and -- I'm sorry, and roughly half were totally destroyed, so we're talking something less than a hundred total.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So a little less than a hundred Serb cultural historical monuments were damaged or destroyed in the presence of KFOR when these monuments were supposed to be protected and when there were no war operations in Kosovo. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I have a basis for this? What's the relevance to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in a part of his expert report, the witness even concluded that the aim of the attack seems to have been to destroy cultural monuments linked to the Albanian population at a time when war was raging in Kosovo. I would like to know whether a similar number of monuments were destroyed at a time when there were no military operations, and the witness himself said that many of these cultural and historical monuments were protected by FOR. In our subsequent analysis, when we look at whether this was part of some kind of joint plan, this should be kept in mind, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what's your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see how that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it does seem, to me, to be relevant because Mr. Bakrac is suggesting that a lot of monuments can be damaged even when they're being guarded by military forces, and that does seem to be a point relevant to the activities in the earlier part of 1999. So let's hear what the witness has to say about it and we'll assess it in due course. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So could you very briefly restate what the question was, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is: Would I be right in saying that the vast majority of these cultural and historical sites were being guarded by KFOR; and that, in spite of this, they were damaged or destroyed and you yourself drew attention to the need to protect these monuments?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During my visit to Kosovo, I tried to impress on the officials we spoke to in Pristina the need to protect even isolated sites. But the fact is during the first summer after the war and in October when we visited, the principal Baedeker sites, the sites that appear in all the guidebooks, like the Pec patriarchy, the Decani monastery, or Gracanica, or the principal monuments in Prizren. All had KFOR guards in the front of them, as did every Serb church in a village which still had Serb inhabitants. The places where we found Serb churches that had been blown up tended to be isolated, rural settlements that had been abandoned by the Serb population in the initial phase after the war. And I assume that KFOR had its priorities as to where it would place guards. But in places like Drsnik and Dolac, we found nobody. It was empty, and we were actually risking life and limb by climbing through the ruins, which could have very easily had land-mines. So it's not true that they were all guarded at the time. Eventually they realised the sensitivity of the issue and started putting soldiers in front of every church that still stood and even some of the ruined ones. As we know, you know, there were attacks even after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, I have one last question for you, which I'm sure will make Their Honours very happy. In the light of your finding that the aim of the attacks seems to have been to destroy the cultural heritage linked to the Albanian population. I wish to ask you whether the majority of cultural and historical monuments in Kosovo originated from the Ottoman Empire.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a statistic that, you know, I would support. In fact, on the one hand, the Ottoman Empire controlled Kosovo for more than half a millennium, really until 1912. Standing buildings tend to be the most recent ones. So I would say of the standing Orthodox churches, a considerable proportion dates from the 20th century. Some, including parts of the Pecka Patriarchia were constructed during the Ottoman period, and some from the middle ages. Similarly with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It seems we did not understand each other. You said or you mentioned the figure of 600 mosques. Is it true that more than half of those originate from the Ottoman Empire, from Turkish times, and that many of those that were damaged originate from Turkish times?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Riedlmayer: Is it not the Ottoman heritage, is it not equally the heritage of the Serbs and the Albanians and Turks, Egyptians, and others who have been living in the area, and that there was no destruction until the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously all of the architecture of Kosovo is the joint heritage of the people who live there. But certain communities are obviously connected to certain parts of the heritage in different ways than others. Orthodox religious believers, who tend to be mostly the Serb population, clearly attach special importance and symbolism to Orthodox heritage; and likewise, Albanians are attached to their Islamic or Roman Catholic heritage. It is simply a fact that ethnic divisions in the Balkans tend to follow religious lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you point out for me, Mr. Bakrac, where that conclusion is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 6, Your Honour. I think it's the same page in English. The paragraph begins: "Three out of four well-preserved town nucleuses in Kosovo suffered serious damage in the spring." It's the sentence the last in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: They were not quoting the exact wording of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And it goes on to say: "And religious monuments associated with Kosovo's Albanian population ..." And you'll bear in mind, of course, that the charge we are dealing with, in Count 5, is the charge of persecutions, which is not a question so much of culture, in this case, as religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, my name is Toma Fila, together with my colleague Mr. Petrovic. I appear for the accused Mr. Sainovic. I will question you very briefly, and if you give me brief answers you'll be rid of me very soon. I have the impression that you somehow rushed this research of yours. I don't know how else to explain this division into parts of cultural heritage that you have seen, which you suddenly abandon in favour of second-hand sources, whether -- regardless of whether this Court tolerates that or not. Is there any reason -- and of course I agree, your research was worthwhile, it was a very good idea to start it. Is there any reason for suddenly abandoning it? Because I cannot escape that impression.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to point out that, as I mentioned in my report, one of the urgencies that gave rise to this project was the simple fact that there had been war and destruction in Kosovo and winter was coming. And if one had to identify damage, for whatever purpose, whether for the purposes of this Court or for purposes of reconstruction and conservation to save what could be saved, it was very important that information be gathered as expeditiously as possible before winter set in. The reason is that if you have a ruined building and its interior is filled with rubble, when you have the winter snow and rain coming and freezing, it can literally push the walls apart. And so after one or two seasons, even a building that might have been salvageable will no longer be salvageable. So that's why we were in a hurry. But we only had a month to do it in, so we did what we could. And we economised our time in such a way that, for example, with the Orthodox sites we tried to cover those sites that the Orthodox church didn't already have photographs of. And similarly, with the Islamic sites, we picked our documentation in such a way that we would visit the sites that were most endangered and which were also accessible to us. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I have to interrupt you. But it's obviously not the case. My objection is not that you went places but that you didn't go everywhere. That's what I'm asking. You told me that you had to work fast because of the weather and all the other restraints. You don't have to pursue any of that; you are knocking at an open door. What I want to know is why you had to wrap some things up so quickly and thus fail to visit some localities at all. Instead, you used some second-hand sources, such as Mr. Bajgora. I'm not saying that those sources were bad. But why didn't you see those sites personally? Why didn't you photograph them personally? What prevented you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as I mentioned, winter was coming. Our research was in October. In that part of the Balkans, the first snow starts coming in November. The second reason was funding. We had a limited amount of funding and we wanted to make the best use of it. We did make two follow-up visits to Kosovo, to try to fill in some gaps, in 2000 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking this is that I have the impression your quick wrapping up has something to do with the arrest of Mr. Milosevic and I think you were receiving instructions from the Prosecutor to wrap things up as quickly as possible so that the indictment can be supplemented. That is the feeling that I have. If I'm not right, please do not take it personally, but it is still my impression.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Milosevic was pretty much the last thing on our minds, because, as of 1999, the notion that he might be overthrown, arrested and handed over to this Tribunal was a very distant possibility. So, in 2000 and 2001, our main focus had to do with the other parts of the -- the other purposes of the study, which is to assist in reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then that brings me to my next question. Why, then, later did you not continue? We would not then have to ask these questions at all, the kinds of questions like my colleague Mr. Bakrac asked. Why did you say there were Serbian crimes, et cetera. Why didn't you continue your work in the spring? Because snows do start but they also end at some point.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, it was a question of funding; money, the root of all evil and also, unfortunately, the only thing that makes such work possible. But also the fact that, by May of 2000, UNMIK had established its own department of culture, we assumed that UNMIK would be carrying out its own assessment. Also, as time had passed, much of what was still quite evident in October of 1999 would be less and less evident as ruins were cleared, as reconstruction was underway. We tried to follow the situation as best we could, but basically the majority of our field-work and the part that we consider most significant was done in the fall of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Allow me not to agree with your first sentence, because I am a lawyer, I mean, that money is the root of all evil. But let us continue. When you set out from Harvard, you said that you flew to The Hague and talked to the Office of the Prosecutor. What I want to know now - and I don't mind that you talked to the Prosecutor; it's not a sin - why didn't you go to the database? First, to your native country, the USA - and I'll tell you at the end why I'm asking these questions - then to the headquarters of NATO in Brussels, where you could have sought reports as to who they bombed, when they bombed, and what they filmed on the ground in Kosovo during the bombing. I'm sorry to be putting this question to you, because I cannot put it to the Prosecutor, and this is a question that has been bugging me since the beginning of the Milosevic trial. NATO shows us some photographs that are convenient to them, and you used them, too. So the question is: Why didn't you ask from NATO information as to exactly what they bombed, which towns, et cetera? I think my question is clear. I don't want to belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've also answered it for yourself, Mr. Fila, but see if Mr. Riedlmayer can add anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, our procedure actually was --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's an expert, Your Honour, he's not a regular witness, and I cannot influence him, even if I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll be delighted to meet the expert at getting material from NATO. But at any rate, carry on, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was not our procedure for a very simple reason. We proceeded on the basis of allegations. So we took all the allegations from all sources seriously, from the Serbian -- from the Yugoslav government White Book, from the Serbian Orthodox church, from the refugee interviews, and so forth, and we operated on that level. As far as going to interview governments and militaries, as His Honour pointed out, this is not the kind of data they are in the habit of sharing with outsiders. So we never approached them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I know that. I tried, too. My only question is: Did you try to get it? I just want to know how many of us didn't get it. Are you one of those who joined the club of those who sought and didn't get?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used everything that was publicly accessible, as you saw, but we had no illusions that if we went to them that they would let us into their database.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is true of the NATO but also your own country, the USA, which leads the NATO, if my understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no dealings with the government at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My next question would be this: Did you, perhaps, think it useful to visit Paris, as the seat of UNESCO? I'm asking this because you quoted the Ambassador of Yugoslavia to UNESCO, Nada Perisic-Popovic, in her demands concerning restoration of allegedly damaged buildings that suffered from NATO air-strikes. In other words, did you try to get in contact with UNESCO representatives, including the Yugoslav ambassador to UNESCO, who was then in Paris?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. Nada Perisic-Popovic's press conference held at the Yugoslav Cultural Centre in Paris was reported by Agence France-Presse, and I took it off of LexisNexis. Insofar as contacting UNESCO, before we undertook this project, we contacted UNESCO to find out, A, whether they were planning any comprehensive mission to assess what was happening in Kosovo, since we had no intention of duplicating it if they were about to do the same, and they informed us that they didn't. They also informed us that they had no first-hand information about what was happening to cultural heritage in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you went to The Hague, and from The Hague, you went directly to Kosovo. Where? By which route?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We flew from Amsterdam to Skopije, and from Skopije by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Once you came to The Hague, to the Office of the Prosecutor, to get information from the horse's mouth as to what's going on in Serbia, did it not occur to you that you might visit Belgrade as well? Because planes fly from Amsterdam to Belgrade as well, and in Belgrade, at The Academy of Sciences, you could have collected additional information, especially relative to the White Book. Did you try that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we didn't come to the Office of the Prosecutor to find out what was going on in Serbia or anywhere else. The only information we got from the Office of the Prosecutor had to do with protocols and procedure. They, at no point, told us what was going on in Kosovo or instructed us as to how and what we should find. As to Serbia, we had access to all the publications from the Serbian government which was very -- and the Yugoslav government, which were very diligent at publicising this material, both in printed form and in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, it was your assessment that you would not get any additional explanation from the government of Yugoslavia as to how the White Book that you quoted in your report was written. You simply thought you didn't need that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you took that book and read it; the book that you told us about yesterday. That book is not in evidence. I don't have it in English, but I will remind you that you told us yesterday how Serb authorities told you that in Gracanica, the Church of Ascension of Our Lady had been bombed and damaged. And then you and your colleague, with a camera, established that the Serbian authorities were not telling the truth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our aim was not to exonerate NATO or to blacken the name of the Belgrade government. What we were trying to find out is what allegations would pan out and which ones did not. And so we went to Gracanica and we took some photographs. We sent -- we got further information from conservation experts. We talked to the monks, and the information about the damage to the church had been publicised on the Serbian information ministry web site already during the war. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I heard that yesterday. Please do not repeat yourself. We must not waste time. My main objection is: Where did you find in the White Book that the Yugoslav authorities had said that the monastery was damaged by an air-strike, by NATO bombs? Because nobody every said that. Let me tell you what was said exactly. I'll read it. "In the night on the 30th of March, the village of Gracanica was bombed for the third time. Four shells fell 500 metres, that is 1500 feet, away from Gracanica monastery," and that's all. It's not written anywhere that Gracanica was destroyed, damaged, or anything so that you should go camera in hand to establish that it's not true. That's about Gracanica. Nobody in Serbia ever claimed that the NATO destroyed Gracanica. What is your comment? You said one thing and we find in writing something quite different. That's page 226 of the book.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The White Book -- the White Book was not my only source for this. If you look in the footnotes to my report, I cite a number of sources from official bodies in Belgrade, which at various points made allegations. In the case of Gracanica, I remember on one of the Serbian government web sites, blurry photos alleging to show munitions fragments embedded in the walls. I also quite well remember in this very same courtroom one of the amici assisting in the Milosevic case, trying to establish that the paintings had detached from the walls and that there was damage to the historical decoration of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Damaged by shock, that's something different. But you said, yesterday, speaking of the White Book, that the Yugoslav government was claiming, in the White Book, that Gracanica had been damaged. I said that was not correct, and now you confirm that it's not correct -- or I am reading from an inaccurate book. Don't tell me what other sources have said; just show me the White Book where the Yugoslav government claims that the NATO alliance burned, set on fire, damaged, bombed, or whatever the Gracanica monastery. The closest location of damage is 500 metres away from the monastery. Do not quote to me other sources. Just agree with me that it's not written in the White Book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, where is the reference in the report to the White Book being the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that yesterday at this trial. He mentioned it. That's why I picked it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you give that as your --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Let me read it back to you. Footnote 11 of his report, if you can find that. That mentions the White Book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but that footnote doesn't relate to the particular damage we're looking at at the moment, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, in his testimony, he said the monastery was not damaged, contrary to claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the footnote refers to the White Book.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's look further on. You spoke yesterday about the Pec/Peje Patriarchy, saying that it was a great monument in Serbia, for Serbia - to us that's another statement because it's the cradle of all of us - anyway, you said that you went there and it was not established, although the White Book makes allegations that the Pec Patriarchy was hit by a NATO air-strike. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was hit. I said that it was damaged, according to the White Book. There were no claims that it had suffered a direct hit, but that bombing adjacent to it had caused serious damage. And the fact is that people, who are more expert than I, the Italian Conservation Institute carried out a study in which they concluded verbatim that none of the damage they saw was due to anything other than rising groundwater and deferred maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not argue with you on that point. I'm saying the White Book does not state that. The White Book states instead: "In the night on the 31st of March during NATO attacks, the reservoir station of the water-supply system was hit 500 metres from the Pec Patriarchy."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is reading too fast. Could he slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you slow, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I finished, in fact, but I have -- I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've got "The reservoir station of the water-supply system was hit 500 metres from the Pec Patriarchy." Now, is that the end of the quotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that's all the reference to the Pec Patriarchy.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you certain? There are two --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's never said that --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- two volumes of the White Book, and, in addition, as I tried to explain in two footnotes of my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I only have volume 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, volume 2 also has a section on cultural heritage. And in footnotes 9 through 11 of my report, at the very end, I speak of the various sources of allegations from Yugoslavia. I wasn't relying entirely on the White Book.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The thrust of my questions is this: Both in the case of Gracanica and the Pec patriarchy, you said your source of information was the White Book. I am simply saying that's not correct and I have no other point to make here. The next question I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be suitable to interrupt there, Mr. Fila, if you're moving on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our next break now, Mr. Riedlmayer, if you can leave the courtroom again --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, I didn't realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Fila. You finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you were viewing the remnants of the mosque in Kosovska Mitrovica - that's close to a very famous bridge on the Serb side, conditionally speaking - did you experience any problems from Serbian authorities when you wanted to view the remains of that mosque? Did anybody try to prevent you from going there and seeing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with an UNMIK official at the time and was not bothered.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Correct. Because we have information from one Prosecution witness, Mahmut Halimi, that there is a mass grave there where Serbs had buried some Albanians. Did you see anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Riedlmayer, we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00. If you could leave with the usher now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer, or rather, good afternoon. I have only a few questions for you. First of all, something that follows from my colleagues' cross-examination today. At the very beginning of your report, in paragraph 2, subparagraph 1, you mention your investigations concerning buildings which were established to have been seriously damaged by NATO air-strikes. In connection with this, in the following paragraph, you say that there were no signs of damage that could be ascribed to the air-strikes in these buildings. My first question in this respect is what criteria you used to reach this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained our criteria as to the description of the damage. As to the cause of the damage, obviously, it's a little more complex, but I can give you some specific examples. For example, there were allegations concerning the mosque in Pec, which was shown in direct examination, the Barakli Xhamia at the centre of the market in Pec, I believe. This was a mosque which had been alleged to have been hit by air-strikes. We visited the mosque and the dome was intact. The door was charred but intact, and the interior had had very serious fire, fire so intense that the marble revetments on the inside and the marble column supporting the women's balcony had split from the heat, and yet there was no sign at all of blast damage. And without being a military expert, I think it's safe to say that this must have been a fire that was set rather than a fire that resulted from any kind of aerial bombardment. So these kinds of observations -- or, for example, the church that was also shown in direct examination, the church of St. Paraskeva in Drsnik, which was also alleged to have been hit by NATO bombardment. There, too, if you looked at the photographs, you could see the roof was intact, the interior had a small fire set in it, and there were graffiti on the walls; again, not the kind of damage one would expect from aerial bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. But you have said, once more, that you are not a military expert; however, when speaking to my colleague Mr. Bakrac, you said you knew nothing about different kinds of projectiles and weapons. My question is, then: Did you not consider the possibility that a projectile can enter a building from the side rather than through the roof? I'm not now referring to this particular location. My question is a general one.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in the case, all I can do is illustrate with the cases that we investigated. In these two particular cases, there was no sign whatsoever of blast damage, which you would expect from any kind of projectile. I think they're generally meant to do that kind of damage. And, you know, I think one can employ certain common sense criteria, without having to be a technical expert on munitions, to come to certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. Now that we're talking about common sense, one of the sites mentioned in this first paragraph is also the Catholic church of St. Anthony in Djakovica. You mentioned it both yesterday and today when questioned or cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. I apologise for not having the page number in the transcript, but I think there is no doubt that the Catholic priest told you that the damage to the door and windows was caused by a bomb falling from the air; not hitting the building directly, but rather, landing in its immediate vicinity. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what he told me. Basically he told me they were expelled. The Yugoslav military occupied the building. And when they returned in May, they found the building damaged. Since he wasn't present, he couldn't tell whether that damage was done by those who were in the building or others. The same goes, I assume, with regard to any other loss of property or damage involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this not the case where you attributed the damage to the windows to blasts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let's differentiate. There was -- there's the church, which was a major monument built in the 19th century --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and adjacent to it, a modern rectory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of them were near the Yugoslav military base. What the priest told me was that, before the bombing happened, about a half an hour before, the military came and expelled him and the nuns from the premises. After it was over, the only damage to the church were some shattered windows. In the case of the rectory, it had been vandalised and pillaged. The allegation that I was -- that moved me to examine these premises was an allegation that the building of the church had been hit by NATO bombs; and in fact, there was no damage. I went inside and outside and it looked in good condition. There was another church a couple hundred metres down the street, which was disused and which they were planning to rebuild but hadn't, which did suffer some damage from air blast. But no allegations concerning that were ever raised by any party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But did you not say earlier today that there was -- I thought it was that church, where the windows --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The windows were blown out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Blown out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is the one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.2 of your report, you mention kulla and the destruction, or rather, you mention towers and that towers were the main subject of attack, the main targets. They were perfect for the KLA to engage in military activity from them, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was already examine -- addressed in the

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: same contention. And my reply to that is that these kulla, most of which were built before World War I, were indeed used as refuges during times of insecurity and especially during blood feuds. But while they were an adequate defence against muskets and hunting rifles, they stood absolutely no chance against modern weapons. In the case of several kulla, where I talked to the owners who said that they had fled to the slopes above and watched the destruction of their kullas, they said the kullas were destroyed by a single projectile held -- hit from a hand-held device, fired into the flammable roof structure, which was enough to cause the whole thing to burn down and collapse. So in a redoubt in late 20th century warfare, they had absolutely no utility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But, Mr. Riedlmayer, my question was: Were these suitable places to shoot from? I wasn't asking about the kind of weapons that might be used to destroy them. On pages 28, 29, and 30 of yesterday's transcript, you mentioned two new references not available to you when you testified in the Milosevic trial, and these are publications by Mr. Krasnici and Mr. Krunic. In the course of yesterday, I glanced through these publications. Mr. Krasnici says that the main purpose of these kullas was defensive; that they were two or three storeys high; that usually the ground floor was built of stone; and that instead of windows they had loop-holes. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like many -- the principal purpose of these was to serve as shelter for people and animals. Like many pre-modern buildings in Europe, the animals and the people generally lived under one roof. The people lived under the upper storeys, which had windows; the lower storeys were used for storage of provisions and stables for the animals. Now, since the kullas did also have this defensive purpose, they had openings on the lower storeys, which could of course be used for shooting. But the fact is that since they were so vulnerable, I think they would make very poor redoubts in any kind of modern warfare. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. I'll move on now. In A2.3 of your report on page 19, you speak about information received from the Kosovo Islamic community, and you say that in some cases verbal descriptions of the extent of the damage were exaggerated. And then you say that the dates given for construction should be taken with caution because they often refer to the date when the foundation was laid, rather than when the building was finished. So you were provided with this information that had to be checked. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to destruction, this was a problem with all the religious communities, including the Serbian Orthodox church. They tended to speak of destruction in very general terms and did not have a very specific vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you need to elaborate on this. If counsel wants more information, Mr. Riedlmayer, he can ask for it. Because you've dealt with this ad longum yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during the examination-in-chief, page 26, lines 1 to 4, when answering Mr. Hannis's questions, you said that evidently if a building was damaged by a projectile and there was a strong blast, there would be holes in the walls and bullet traces on all side; and that in that case, it would be logical to conclude that such damage was not caused in peacetime. Also, when you testified in the Milosevic case, you spoke about the mosque in Djakovica. And on page 26, lines 18 and forward, you said that the minaret had been toppled and that you could see several small round holes in it. Can you describe these holes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I already described them in court here. They were approximately maybe 30 centimetres, 40 centimetres across. I can't give you an exact measurement, since I was looking at them from the ground up. There were approximately four or five of them in the part of the minaret that was still standing. The top of the minaret above the balcony had been sheared off. They looked like the kinds of holes that might be made by some kind of projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was insufficiently precise. The first part of yesterday's transcript, which I quoted, is one from which it follows that you saw bullet -- traces of bullets on all sides in some locations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some locations, I saw buildings that had clearly been shot up by small arms. This was, by far, the minority of cases. And it wasn't always clear whether this was a building caught in some sort of battle or cross-fire or whether it was an act of vandalism. I can give you an example of the latter in Pec where I visited the mosque called, in Albanian, Xhamija e Kuqe, the red mosque, which had been burnt down. And since it wasn't listed in the literature, I was looking for some kind of inscription to figure out what it was called in Baedeker. And I found an Islamic an inscription on the fountain right next to the mosque, part of complex. And somebody had clearly emptied a whole clip into the inscription. All the bullet impacts were in the Arabic inscription on top of the fountain. So clearly that's not the mark of a battle, but somebody getting very angry about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there other sites where you saw traces of bullets which might be the traces of battles?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't from memory cite any specifically, but there were buildings that were badly destroyed where you did indeed see sprays of bullets in the wall. I would need to have my database in front of me to hunt it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. One last question on this topic. You testified in the Milosevic case. And on pages 2684, lines 21 to 22, you said, "We saw no signs that the mosques had been hit by small calibre weapons." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the transcript in front of me, so I can't comment on the context thereof. But I can say in general, when we saw mosques which had suffered damage, we didn't see -- it was very uncommon to see any kind of small-calibre impacts. And you would expect that, for example, if someone's trying to take down a sniper, the most efficient way is, obviously, to try and shoot him down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Riedlmayer. My name is Dan Ivetic and I am one of the attorneys for Mr. Lukic in these proceedings, and I've got some questions to ask you. I'll try to move along quickly and not repeat items that have already been dealt with, since we have time constraints. Now, I'd first like to ask you, you've been asked and you've specified several times that you are not a military expert. I have some other questions about your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you kindly slow down a little bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So much for trying to speed things up. I'll try and keep it slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've been asked, and you've answered, about your lack of any military expertise. I would like to ask you about other areas of expertise that I believe are relevant to some of the work you did. Now, first of all, sir, am I correct that you never had any formal education or training in the fields of fire-scene or bomb-scene investigations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I'm not an arson investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you did not, in fact, employ or consult with any such expert while you were in the field, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, I could tell you that, in the course of my investigations both in Kosovo and in Bosnia, I have seen, in person, several hundred sites and, on photographs, several hundred more sites about which I had other information and have accumulated a fair degree of experience. And I've also been reading the technical literature. So, to a certain extent, I have become self-educated in this. But I have no technical training in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what about forensic structural engineering? You haven't had any formal education or training in that field, have you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a structural engineer and we did not try to do structural testing; however, I was accompanied in my field-work in Kosovo by Mr. Herscher, who is a trained architect and who is qualified to make some judgements about the buildings, based on visual inspection. As I said, we had no means to carry out technical tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. Herscher is an architect; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree with me that, in order to definitively, as an expert, give descriptions of and make conclusions of exactly in what manner these buildings and mosques were damaged, you would need to have had the assistance of such an expert, that is to say, a bomb-scene or fire-scene investigations expert and a forensic structural engineer, as the literature indicates?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the best of all circumstances, that's what you would hope to have; however, in our field survey, we had much more modest goals and those were, I think, achievable through simple visual observation and application of certain basic criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And you've already talked about the modest goals and the results obtained, so I'm not going to ask you about that. Now, if we can turn to your factual findings on the ground and your knowledge and experience, you've mentioned Bosnia. Would you still agree with your assessment that you stated during the Milosevic proceedings, at page 2714, lines 18 through 21, that as far as the Balkans were concerned, "the biggest driving force for desecration and looting of religious sites was quite aside from any political motives and boiled down to just simple human greed."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the reference in front of me, so I don't know the exact context. But as far as I can recall the remark, it was addressed to the fact that, in many of these cases, before a site was destroyed, it was looted. So, for example, in the case of Vucitrn, the market mosque was surrounded by the goldsmith's bazaar, all the shops being endowments of the mosque, meaning the rental income of the shops supported the mosque. And before it was all burned down, according to local residents, the goldsmith's shops were systematically looted and then set on fire. So I think when people talk about ideology or ethnic hatreds or troops getting out of control, what they neglect to mention is the profit motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you've answered my other question, which was going to be if you agreed that this applied to Kosovo and Metohija. I take it from your response, citing an example in Kosovo, that you do agree that human greed and profit motive had a role potentially --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly had some role.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based upon my reading of the Milosevic proceedings and the transcript therefrom, it's my understanding that at that point in time, while you were being cross-examined, you learned for the first time that certain information that you had received, particularly from Djakovica, came from KLA members, specifically one Petrik Domi, who was a member of the 124th Brigade of the KLA. Now, since the Milosevic case, have you done any more work to check and determine if any of your other informants or sources had any compromising or potentially compromising ties with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph you referred to was one that was shown in court here. It showed the Djakovica market on fire. Now, I didn't acquire it directly from Mr. Domi, I acquired it from the news agency which distributed it in 1999. It was clearly just one piece among several pieces of evidence on the destruction of the bazaar, and, you know, if you throw it out, I don't think it would change my assessment. I'd leave it, obviously, to the Court to determine what utility it has. I only received very few photos from individuals. Most of them came from the religious communities or other institutional sources, but all the individuals are named.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This individual is named in relation to one of your sites, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's named as a source of one photograph of the burning market. He is a resident of Djakovica and claims to have taken that photograph while the market was being burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your source of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- your copy was Reuters, I think you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it came from a news agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, to clear up something that my colleague Mr. Hannis, I think, misspoke about yesterday, you were talking of kullas and Mr. Hannis asked you if, in fact, the family compounds, as he called them, that we had heard about in other evidence were, in fact, kullas. Now, am I correct that not all family compounds on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija are, indeed, kullas; that, in fact, there are ordinary residences that are built as compounds?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both rural Albanians and, to some extent, rural Serbs lived in extended families. They're known in the Balkans as zadrugas. And they often are built as compounds, several houses within a walled enclosure. In the areas we're talking about, western Kosovo and northern Kosovo, this is where kullas are concentrated. But family compounds can be found anywhere in Kosovo, and very often they consist of modern buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And without having reviewed the evidence that Mr. Hannis was generally speaking of, you would have no way of knowing whether the family compounds that are relevant to this case and to other witnesses were, indeed, kullas or these residences, these zadrugas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the sites were identified by name -- the kullas had been studied in the literature, so you could know, for example, the old town of Decani was almost entirely composed of kullas, as was the town of Junik. There are entire villages which are almost exclusively kullas. In other places, you know, I wouldn't expect to see kullas, for example, down in the south of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you expect -- I have to slow down since we both speak English. If I cut in right after your answer, the interpreters have trouble. Would you expect a person testifying about a compound to use the word -- would it be -- would they use the word "kulla"? Would that be the way of differentiating between a zadruga and a kulla?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a zadruga -- I'm sorry, I should slow down. Zadruga is simply the name of the extended family; it's not the name of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So extended families can live in modern apartment buildings, if you like. But I can't speak for what a witness would say. If you asked them what type of house it would be, if it was a kulla, they would probably identify it as such. My study was not based on those incidents; it simply notes that of the extant kullas in Kosovo, which various experts estimate around 500, some 90 percent were destroyed in 1998/1999, which seems a very high proportion. It is certainly borne out by local studies, like the one carried out by UNMIK, Urban Institute in Pec, which found that in the municipality of Decani, for example, out of 260-odd kullas, 230 had been damaged or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hate to cut you short, sir, but I'm try to finish you and leave time for the Prosecution for re-direct. So I apologise if I seem to speed along on some thing. You already talked, I think at length, with my colleagues about whether or not these kullas could be used for -- for battle purposes. Now -- and the question I want to ask you is: With respect to that, you answered that you talked with people who told you how the kullas had been damaged or destroyed. Now, I want to ask you: Is it correct that you cannot actually definitively exclude that some of these instances may be misreported to you, to serve propaganda goals of the KLA and protect the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exclude anything, seeing as I didn't take statements under oath. However, I can tell you that in these specific cases, I'm talking of a village called Gornje Streoce, just between Decani and Pec. That's S-t-r-e-o-c-e. The kullas had no bullet-holes on them and they were completely gutted with fire, which seems consistent with what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday we went through the -- actually, I guess today as well, we went through the extracts from your report that talked about a variety of sites. And based upon my rough calculation, it would appear that a majority of them, or some seven or eight of the sites, come from -- come from this Sabri Bajgora in the IMG database listed as the surveyors, which you listed today as shorthand for the source of information. Now, am I correct that this IMG database actually does not contain any information relating to how a particular building was damaged; it only contains information as to the extent of the damage and the costs to repair the same?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So then would it be fair to say that the bulk of the information as to how these structures were damaged came from this Sabri Bajgora?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as there is specific information as to when and by whom, it would come from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And obviously --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say it looks like it's been burned, that may come from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And as far as this Islamic community headed by Mr. Bajgora, you don't know whether in fact they conducted any interviews, if at all, or whether they relied upon newspaper accounts or media accounts, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were newspaper or media accounts, I suspect if it was international ones I would have seen them. What I do know, from talking to Mr. Bajgora, is that in July and August and September, for the three months after the end of the war, he said he was continually on the road visiting the various local Islamic communities, taking pictures, and collecting information on what had happened to his communities' properties during the war. So, yes, he did do field-work. So what extent he corroborated this from other sources, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I assume that his main information was firsthand, talking to local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicate there that if there had been media accounts; you suspect you would have seen them. There are at least several occasions in the excerpts where -- for cites that you received information from Mr. Bajgora, you also had newspaper accounts. My question for you is: If, in fact, it turns out that Mr. Bajgora used those same newspaper accounts for reaching his conclusions, the newspaper accounts that you cited can't really be corroborative or cross-referencing Mr. Bajgora's claims, can they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly one way of looking at it. The fact is that the instances, where I have newspaper accounts, are mainly limited to a few cites that were particularly notorious and which, therefore, attracted the attention of the international press. I doubt, actually, that in the circumstances prevailing in Kosovo in the immediate aftermath of the war, that Mr. Bajgora or his community would have been so clued in to the international press. There was no power and no telephone communication, and in all of Pristina there was one internet cafe charging outrageous rates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can ask you about one particular site that you did visit, the Rogovo site, the Xhamija e Hasan Ages, that you visited with Mr. Herscher -- I apologise. That's P1784, if anyone wishes to follow along. Now, in that damage description, the last line of that says: "Village site of 29 January 1999 MUP operation in which 24 Albanians were killed." Now, I note that there is no reference to Sabri Bajgora, there are no media accounts, and the informant's statement from an unnamed storekeeper does not mention anything from this January of 1999 incident.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The January of 1999 incident was widely publicised at the time in news accounts. But I had no idea what they were going to include in the final indictment. I simply put this in, essentially saying, "Here it is if you're" -- "if it's of any interest." But, you know, whether the destruction of the mosque actually happened subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. That's what the -- at least what the informant states. So this is put in here simply to assist the Prosecutor in its other investigations and is not part of your -- of the task that you were --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- the primary task of your --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And it was put in the at the last moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.
