Now, for each of these incidents that we've gone now for two days of damage to specific sites, you cannot positively exclude the possibility or the fact that if these acts were done intentionally, the damage may be the spontaneous reaction due to angry, rage, or greed of local Serb inhabitants, either responding to attacks of NATO or the KLA, can you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, I believe many of the reported incidents, at least according to the newspaper accounts and the informants' information of when the damage occurred, most of them occurred, if not all occurred, after, immediately after, NATO attacks had commenced. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot speak to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in fact, where the manpower and facilities were available -- or should I say: Did you have knowledge of the fact that, when manpower and facilities were available, the Serb authorities actually tried to protect and control such Islamic religious sites from mob activity during the course of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. For instance, had you heard or did you inquire about the Prizren mosque? First of all, are you familiar with the mosque in Prizren that is considered to be the central landmark and symbol of the Islamic community in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Sinan Pasha mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the fact that they Serbian police posted, in the city of Prizren, guards on a daily basis to protect and secure that mosque from any potential mob activity on the part of the local populace?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard that. I did hear that, during the war, both the prayer in the mosques and the call to prayer were forbidden in Prizren. This is according to Mr. Virmica, when I spoke to him. He lives in Prizren. But he never said anything about guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday, when testifying about a picture that you bought from a journalist - I forget the name of the journalist, but it was relating to Pristina - you stated in your sworn testimony here that on June 15th, 1999, hours before the arrival of the KFOR units, I believe it was the Islamic library that was set on fire by Serbian police, who ran into the building and ran out. Now, again, we have no source for that, and, in fact, I did not see it referenced in any of the exhibits that were tendered from your report. So, first of all, what was the source of this information? Was it the news journalist who sold you the photographs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually another news account which is in my database. I don't believe it was among the pages from the database that was entered into evidence. The photograph was by a Reuters photographer named Oleg Popov. And I didn't buy it from him, I bought it from the Reuters archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of the fact, sir, that as far as Pristina is concerned, the first KFOR contingents arrived there already on June the 12th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have had the date wrong, and I believe I indicated that in court because I'm speaking from memory. But the burning of the Islamic archive, which is what it was - it was the archive where all the property records of the Islamic community and other documents were held - did happen in the hours before the arrival of KFOR in Pristina. It wasn't -- it doesn't hang on a single photograph. There was news footage on various outlets, from CNN to BBC, showing the burning building. It was a widely reported thing, because reporters were coming in in advance of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Footage showing the burning building but not the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but the reporters interviewed people who had seen the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the course of your personal interviews with informants and sources for your study, isn't it true that you came across instances when persons had misrepresented things to you, trying to actually blame Serbs for damage to sites that, in fact, were damaged in some other way?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was at least one instance of that. It wasn't connected to buildings, but in Vucitrn there were some smashed tombstones. And initially, when I talked to residents, some children said, "Oh, it must have been the Serbs," and then some others said, "No, this just happened last week" and that it was done at the behest of an aid agency from the United Arab Emirates who were working on some sort of fanatical sect. So there were some smashed tombstones. But that's the only instance I know where people were falsely attributing it. Similarly, in Djakovica, there was one other instance where there was a foundation of a mosque and a minaret standing but no mosque. And somebody tried to tell me that this was ruined in the war, and then I asked the Islamic community and they said, "No, it was an old mosque. We tore it just before the war and had intentions to reconstruct it." But these are the only two instances I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me go back for a moment to Vucitrn to try and refresh your recollection some, because I think we're talking about the same instance but you've got a couple things turned around in there. The Prosecution tendered today a new exhibit, P2456, and on the fifth page of that, it talks -- this is the report from your database talking about the Gazi Ali Bej mosque in Vucitrn. And according to that, it says: "Old man encountered in mosque courtyard initially tried to blame Serbs for damage to cemetery but several young people said that that was not true," and then it goes on to give the part that you had mentioned. So you, in fact, had heard the mistruth not from children, as you had said here, but from an old man. Does that sound more like the --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the -- and then it was corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thankfully it was corrected by persons who had actually seen the damage being done at the bequest of the aid agency. Now, the question I have for you is: Based upon this experience, you cannot, therefore, exclude the possibility that some of the other statements you heard, particularly where there was only one person involved, were, likewise, attempts at misrepresentation, can you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I only recorded what was told to me. I did not depose people under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as far as some of the other informants or news accounts that you relied upon in reaching your reports, I find some, in particular, inconsistent with one another and I'll very briefly summarise. The one, in particular, I'm talking about is Exhibit P1781 dealing with the Hadum mosque and bazaar in Djakovica. According to the excerpt from your database that was submitted into evidence, one informant says that Serb police and civilians are to blame for this damage. The other informant that you had in that case said Serb police and military, but makes no mention of civilians, were responsible. And finally, the news report, based upon multiple accounts by Chris Stephen, from The New York Times, says very explicitly that 50 persons in military uniforms alone did the act. Now, sir, all I want to ask you about the inconsistencies is to confirm that you are not in a position, based upon the knowledge that you collected, to reconcile these different accounts, are you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is why I included them, as they stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And, in fact, if we can focus for a moment on the essay by Chris Stephen from The New York Times, you only have an excerpt included in there. Do you recall, from reading that article, that immediately after your excerpt in his essay, he describes how the old town where the mosque and bazaar were located were "the epicenter of Kosovo Liberation Army activity, a haven for guerillas at war with the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, but it was seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you recall, or do you know, that, in fact, a KLA headquarters was located precisely in that part of Djakovica city, precisely in March of 1999, as the article that you have identified as a source also indicates?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used it as a source only for what it had to say about the building. I was not particularly interested in the other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have an exhibit number for the rest of the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have it because I thought that I couldn't use it, given that I did not know of the article until last night, which was obviously after I could have given notice of it. So I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that should be put into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just the excerpts that I've talked about, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the additional excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got part of the report here and you're supplementing that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so that should be put into the system and the Chamber notified, in writing, of its number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do that, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that, actually, is the last question I had for this witness, so hopefully we have time to finish him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis. I mean, you have some time if -- if you just give me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since there is no other case in this courtroom this afternoon, we can allow Judge Nosworthy to depart for her other case and we can sit, under 15 bis, a little longer to enable us to clear up issues over exhibits and complete the re-direct. It's only going to take five or ten minutes, I image, and -- Mr. Hannis, you look doubtful about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of what just happened with supplementing the newspaper article, there was some questions put to this witness concerning the White Book and some of the sources of the Yugoslav authorities and the Yugoslav web sites concerning damage that this witness relied on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I had proposed to introduce some of those documents, or portions of those documents, to supplement what was asked him on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're given half an hour, would you manage, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I could do it in the amount of time if I could find the material, but I don't have it all at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have a witness here who you anticipated would be two days and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can accommodate that and it's disappointing that you can't. Does it help if we break briefly and do this? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- or is that not going to be of much assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that could be of assistance to me. Your Honour, I guess if I can inquire of the witness, if it's inconvenient for him to return tomorrow. I don't know what his travel arrangements are. I would defer to him because he's come here on numerous occasions in the past and I'll adjust my schedule to his.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My return flight is booked for Friday, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's regrettable, Mr. Hannis, that we can't make use of these -- the opportunity when it's there to get everything heard at the one time and help our understanding of the situation. But if it's got to be tomorrow, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Riedlmayer, you'll need to return, I'm afraid, tomorrow to resume at 9.00. And, again, please bear in mind what I said about no discussion about the evidence meanwhile. You may leave the courtroom now and we will see you at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
